pages.text: Akorfa’s science club was making a poster about pangolins, shy, scaly mammals that live in Ghana’s forests. Beside one picture she wrote ENDANGERED. Her friend Obed asked a question that stopped them both: ‘What if the last one is gone? Is that it for ever?’
sentences: Akorfa’s science club was making a poster about pangolins, shy, scaly mammals that live in Ghana’s forests.
Beside one picture she wrote ENDANGERED.
Her friend Obed asked a question that stopped them both: ‘What if the last one is gone?
Is that it for ever?’
pages.alt: Two students beside a poster of a pangolin with the word ENDANGERED.

pages.text: At the library, Akorfa read about the Frozen Zoo in San Diego, in the United States. Since 1975, scientists there have kept living cells from animals in tanks at about −196 °C. It now holds over 11,500 cell lines from more than 1,300 species and subspecies. ‘A zoo with no animals walking about,’ said Obed. ‘Only cells.’
sentences: At the library, Akorfa read about the Frozen Zoo in San Diego, in the United States.
Since 1975, scientists there have kept living cells from animals in tanks at about −196 °C.
It now holds over 11,500 cell lines from more than 1,300 species and subspecies.
‘A zoo with no animals walking about,’ said Obed.
‘Only cells.’
pages.alt: A girl reads a book about a frozen zoo with a picture of cold storage tanks.

pages.text: Why cells and not whole animals? They asked Madam Tawiah, who answered with a question: ‘What happens to living things when you freeze them?’ The club froze slices of tomato overnight in the school freezer, then thawed them. The slices came out soft and watery.
sentences: Why cells and not whole animals?
They asked Madam Tawiah, who answered with a question: ‘What happens to living things when you freeze them?’ The club froze slices of tomato overnight in the school freezer, then thawed them.
The slices came out soft and watery.
pages.alt: Students lift thawed tomato slices from a tray, which look soft and collapsed.

pages.text: Under a hand lens, fresh tomato looked firm and neat. The thawed slice looked collapsed. ‘Ice crystals can form inside cells and tear them open,’ Akorfa read. Then how do scientists freeze cells and keep them alive? ‘They use special liquids called cryoprotectants, and cool the cells carefully, so far less damage is done.’
sentences: Under a hand lens, fresh tomato looked firm and neat.
The thawed slice looked collapsed.
‘Ice crystals can form inside cells and tear them open,’ Akorfa read.
Then how do scientists freeze cells and keep them alive?
‘They use special liquids called cryoprotectants, and cool the cells carefully, so far less damage is done.’
pages.alt: Two slices of tomato under a magnifying lens, one firm and one collapsed.

pages.text: Banked cells have already been put to work. Scientists have produced clones of a black-footed ferret and a Przewalski’s horse from cells that were frozen decades earlier. ‘So we can bring animals back!’ said Obed. Akorfa shook her head. ‘A clone is one animal. A species needs many animals with different genes to stay healthy.’
sentences: Banked cells have already been put to work.
Scientists have produced clones of a black-footed ferret and a Przewalski’s horse from cells that were frozen decades earlier.
‘So we can bring animals back!’ said Obed.
Akorfa shook her head.
‘A clone is one animal.
A species needs many animals with different genes to stay healthy.’
pages.alt: A friend and Akorfa discuss a picture of a horse and a ferret with small question marks.

pages.text: They tried a thought experiment. Freeze the cells of one pangolin, then lose its forest. ‘Where would a baby pangolin live? What would it eat?’ asked Obed. ‘Ants and termites,’ said Akorfa. ‘That is a forest job, not a freezer job.’
sentences: They tried a thought experiment.
Freeze the cells of one pangolin, then lose its forest.
‘Where would a baby pangolin live?
What would it eat?’ asked Obed.
‘Ants and termites,’ said Akorfa.
‘That is a forest job, not a freezer job.’
pages.alt: A pangolin in a green forest with ants on a tree beside a drawing of an empty freezer.

pages.text: Akorfa rewrote the poster: Freezers keep cells. Forests keep lives. The club listed ways to help: learn about pangolins, protect the places they live, and tell adults to report trapping or selling to wildlife officers.
sentences: Akorfa rewrote the poster: Freezers keep cells.
Forests keep lives.
The club listed ways to help: learn about pangolins, protect the places they live, and tell adults to report trapping or selling to wildlife officers.
pages.alt: Students paint a new poster with a forest and a freezer side by side.

pages.text: In her notebook Akorfa wrote: ‘A frozen cell bank is like a pause button, not a rescue. It gives time and insurance, but only if we also protect the places where animals live. What we do not know yet is whether banked cells can ever rebuild a wild population.’ Obed added a question mark. The end.

activities.question: What does the Frozen Zoo keep in its cold tanks?
options: Living cells from many animal species

activities.prompt: Predict: what will a tomato slice look like after one night in a freezer and then thawing?

activities.question: Why can ordinary freezing damage living cells?
options: Ice crystals can form inside them and tear them
The cold makes cells grow too fast
activities.explanation: Ice crystals inside cells can break them, so cell banks use cryoprotectants and careful cooling.

activities.definition: Special liquids that protect cells from ice damage when they are frozen.

activities.question: Why is a frozen cell bank not enough to save pangolins?
options: Animals also need habitat, food and many different individuals
Cells cannot be frozen at all

activities.prompt: Put the club’s thinking in order.
items: Ask what happens if the last animal is gone.
Test what freezing does to living cells.
Decide that habitat matters as much as cell banks.

activities.prompt: Akorfa felt hopeful about science but worried about forests. When have you felt two feelings about the same news?

glossary.definition: In danger of disappearing for ever.
The tiny living building blocks of animals, plants and people.
Special liquids that protect cells from ice damage during freezing.
Animals grown from the cells of another animal, with the same genes.
